question: In recent months, the inhabitants of Chios have been troubled by the Greek Government’s upcoming plans to mine for antimony (surface and underground mining) in a forest area on the boundaries of Natura site GR4130003. The map of the area where the mining will take place includes villages, settlements, a hot spring and baths and there are concerns about the impact the mining activities will have on the water table.
Meanwhile, antimony mines in China are closing due to the stricter environmental requirements introduced in the country.

Recital 17 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 on ensuring a secure and sustainable (EU) supply of critical raw materials states that to ensure the sustainability of the production of critical raw materials, new projects should be planned and implemented sustainably, including ensuring environmental protection and the prevention and minimisation of socially adverse impacts through transparent business practices.
In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the mining activities in northern Chios and their impact on the environment, social cohesion and the quality of the island’s drinking water?
Has the Commission considered antimony recycling or the parallel process of extracting antimony from mined copper, lead and gold, as is the practice worldwide?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.3.2025) 1. Yes, the Commission has been made aware of this. The EU policy on critical raw materials1 aims to ensure a secure and sustainable supply of critical raw materials while not weakening the environmental and social rules.

Projects should be planned and implemented covering all aspects of sustainability highlighted in the publication ‘EU principles for sustainable raw materials’2. The environmental effects of projects covering mining activities have to be duly assessed in accordance with EU requirements as the Habitats Directive3 or the Water Framework Directive4.

In view of the Commission's powers as guardian of the Treaties, it will make every effort to ensure that the environmental and social standards set are respected. 2. The supply of primary antimony is heavily concentrated in a few countries. Therefore, recycling plays a crucial role to ensure secure and sustainable supply of antimony.

Secondary antimony is mainly recovered from lead-acid batteries and to a lesser extent from polymers5. The Commission aims to increase such recycling efforts by setting the right legal framework in the critical raw materials, waste and product legislation but also by funding several projects to develop innovative antimony recovery processes6.

According to the Extractive Waste Directive7, operators of extractive waste facilities draw up a waste management plan, which have the objective to encourage the recovery of extractive waste by means of recycling, reusing or reclaiming such waste in accordance with the existing environmental standards.
